visual.text: THE BORROW SHED · VOID DECK, BLOCK 318
You need a hole in the wall, not a drill in the cupboard.
Borrow the tool. Finish the job. Bring it back.
A cupboard under a staircase with open doors, showing rows of drills, ladders and spanners, each with a numbered tag. A handwritten sign on the door reads ‘Take what you need. Return what you took.’

Most tools in a home are used for a few minutes a year and spend the rest of their lives gathering dust. The Borrow Shed is a shared cupboard run by residents, for residents. Borrow a ladder to change a light bulb, a pump for your bicycle, or a sewing machine to hem new curtains — free, for up to three days.

visual.title: Three steps
items: Scan the tag on the tool with your phone
Take it home and use it with care
Wipe it clean and hang it back on the same hook

questions.text: Look at the headline: ‘You need a hole in the wall, not a drill in the cupboard.’ What does it suggest about owning tools?

scheme.answer: People only need a tool for the short job it does, so there is no need to buy one and keep it at home.
accept: What matters is getting the job done, not having your own tool, so borrowing makes more sense than buying.

seeds.text: It suggests that people only need the tool to do one job, so they do not really need to buy and keep one at home.
What you want is the job done, not the tool itself, so owning it is unnecessary and you can just borrow.
It suggests that drills should not be stored inside cupboards.
It suggests that people should not make holes in their walls.
It suggests something about tools at home.
You need a hole in the wall, not a drill in the cupboard.

questions.text: Besides free tools, what other benefit of the Borrow Shed does Mrs Kaur’s experience show?

scheme.answer: The volunteers on duty teach borrowers how to use the tools safely.
accept: Borrowers get help and guidance from a neighbour who knows how to use the tools.
Residents can learn new skills from the volunteers.

questions.text: In the picture, a handwritten sign reads ‘Take what you need. Return what you took.’ What does the sign tell us the Borrow Shed expects of the people who use it?

scheme.answer: It expects borrowers to be honest and responsible, taking only what they need and bringing every tool back.
accept: It trusts residents to return the tools they borrow.

seeds.text: It expects them to be honest and responsible and bring back whatever tools they borrowed.

questions.text: What is the purpose of the last line: ‘Have a tool you never use? Donate it and let it work for the whole block.’?

scheme.answer: To encourage residents to give their unused tools to the Borrow Shed so that all their neighbours can use them.
accept: To get more tools for the shed by asking residents to donate the ones they do not need.
